Conceptual meaning: Foundational, conceptual knowledge of what AI/ML is, how it works, and its underlying mechanics, typically delivered through curricula or introductory/experiential exposure
Included existing topics: Topic 4 (School curriculum, machine learning, and STEM-oriented AI education); Topic 7 (Children, games, creative activities, and experiential AI learning); Topic 0 (AI literacy competencies, educator readiness, and ethical understanding) [also fits Evaluating/Judging]
Justification: Topics 4 and 7 foreground explaining AI concepts (machine learning, curriculum design, game-based/experiential exposure) rather than using AI tools directly. Topic 0's top terms ('understanding', 'competencies', 'curriculum', 'assessment') center on defining and building conceptual literacy, though its ethical-understanding component also has an evaluative dimension (see note).

Conceptual meaning: Direct, hands-on use of generative AI systems as tools — prompting, conversing with, or co-writing with models
Included existing topics: Topic 5 (ChatGPT, writing, language learning, and prompting); Topic 3 (Generative AI literacy and instructional tool integration) [also fits Adopting AI]
Justification: Topic 5's top terms ('chatgpt', 'writing', 'prompt', 'llms') describe literacy as the practice of interacting with a generative system. Topic 3 similarly centers on hands-on instructional integration of generative tools, but because it also concerns institutional/curricular uptake, it is cross-listed under Adopting AI.

Conceptual meaning: Psychological and behavioral determinants of whether and how individuals take up AI technologies: self-efficacy, perceived usefulness, anxiety, trust in one's own capability, behavioral intention
Included existing topics: Topic 1 (Self-efficacy, acceptance, anxiety, and AI adoption factors); Topic 3 (Generative AI literacy and instructional tool integration) [also fits Interacting with AI]
Justification: Topic 1 is explicitly framed around acceptance/adoption constructs (self-efficacy, intention, perceived usefulness, anxiety) drawn from technology-acceptance research, distinct from the act of using AI itself. Topic 3 is cross-listed here because 'instructional tool integration' concerns institutional/curricular adoption of generative AI, not only the interactional act of using it.

Conceptual meaning: Critical, ethical, and epistemic appraisal of AI systems and their outputs: trust, decision-making authority, bias, human oversight, professional/ethical judgment
Included existing topics: Topic 6 (Human decision-making, trust, and public-facing AI systems); Topic 2 (Higher education integration, ethics, and professional practice) [also fits Situated/institutional]; Topic 0 (AI literacy competencies, educator readiness, and ethical understanding) [also fits Understanding AI]
Justification: Topic 6's top terms ('decision', 'trust', 'ethical', 'human', 'public') center on evaluating AI's role in decisions and public systems. Topic 2 combines higher-education integration with an explicit ethics/critical-practice component, so it is cross-listed under Situated/institutional AI literacy. Topic 0's 'ethical' and 'assessment' terms give it a judgment component alongside its conceptual-understanding core.

Conceptual meaning: AI literacy as constituted within a specific professional domain, institution, or occupational role, rather than as a general competency
Included existing topics: Topic 8 (Healthcare and medical AI literacy); Topic 9 (Libraries, librarians, and information services); Topic 2 (Higher education integration, ethics, and professional practice) [also fits Evaluating/judging]
Justification: Topics 8 and 9 are organized entirely around domain-specific institutional contexts (clinical/healthcare settings; library and information services) rather than a general topical theme. Topic 2's 'higher education integration' and 'professional practice' language reflects the same situated/institutional framing, alongside its ethics component (see Evaluating/judging).
